cases.rationale: gxh4 changes whether ...Bxf1 can win the exchange and the rook entry at c7. The long-term value of the changed king cover is unclear in these lines.
...Qd5, ...Nxe5 and ...h6 lead to distinct checks and threats around the black king. The concrete defence dominates the comparison.
Black has to calculate the rook exchange and the opposing threats of promotion. The connected plans in the rook ending still revolve around the h- and f-pawns after the immediate captures.
Qxf4 takes the loose knight and gives Black a particular ...e5 continuation. The separate long-term influence of the exposed white king is uncertain in this window.
White's d6 pawn constrains Black while f4 and f5 gain space and Black advances the queenside pawns. The queen threatens entry on h6 in some lines, with unclear separate tactical demand.
The rooks and minor pieces manoeuvre around the a-pawn. Several closely scored continuations contain ordinary exchanges and different ways to blockade or advance that pawn.
...d4 opens a concrete line into e2 with a potential exchange sacrifice. The d-pawn advance and open files also govern the other continuations with the rook on a2 or b8.
...d4 forces a choice among queen and minor-piece exchanges. The open d-file and differing White queenside development persist in the quieter reply lines.
...Nd3 brings a concrete attack on e1 and f4. The alternatives allow different captures and forced trades. No independent lasting strategic consideration was established.
Qa1+ and Qb2+ force the king away before b4+ and Ne3+ win the queen on g4. The checks and fork determine this choice.
White has to respond to the threats of ...Nf1 or ...Nxe2. The pressure of the rooks and queenside pawns around White's king continues after the first exchanges.
Rxh1 takes the exposed rook and allows a different material balance after the following exchanges. Black's advanced d-pawn still constrains the rook and bishop in every line.
The c6 and b-pawns fix the rooks' roles. The similar lines include quiet choices and repeated rook manoeuvres, with no verified tactical difference.
Both sides are deciding which pawn to advance and which rook controls the c-file. The leading alternatives lead to different but comparable structures.
White can trade on c1 or maintain pressure on the c-file and defend the second rank. The b-pawn and minor-piece plans persist beyond the ordinary exchanges.
...g5 and ...g4 gain space and displace pieces. ...Bxf3 instead changes White's pawn cover and the later pressure on e5. The tactical importance of these exchanges is uncertain.
The pawn choices fix different queenside structures and influence the knight route to b6. Concrete exchanges occur later, with unclear tactical significance for the first move.
White's knight and bishop can use d6 while rooks occupy the open files. The plausible a4 plan changes pressure on b5. The relative tactical demand is uncertain.
...Nd6 changes whether the ...f4 exchange opens a checking route for a black rook. White still has a dangerous c6 passer and choices about how to support it.
...Qg5 changes the immediate queen-trade and knight threats in each variation. Its strategic meaning after the exchanges is uncertain because the shown alternatives are already losing.
h3 and g4 regain space, Nd5 uses a different central route, and a4 alters the queenside lever. The leading exchanges do not establish an immediate tactical refutation.
White's rooks and queen choose files while Black prepares different pawn breaks. The knight excursions are one of several similar plans for the centre.
...Qh4 and ...Qf6 determine whether White's e-pawn advances or Black can attack with ...Nf3+. The advanced pawns e6 and g3 remain distinct strategic constraints in both branches.
Both sides can contest the c5 square with their knights, while h4 and ...b4 alter the structure on the wings. The closely scored trades on c5 do not show a separate forced gain.
White must account for ...h3+ and ...g3 while advancing the a-pawn. That passer and the placement of the two rooks continue to govern the position after the immediate exchanges.
Rb1, Qxb2 and Rc2 change whether Black can promote and which rooks can enter the second rank. The d- and e-pawn breaks keep influencing the resulting structure.
...Rd2 improves the second-rank rook while ...g5 and ...g6 prepare king and rook activity. The ordinary defences keep the position governed by open files and pawn weaknesses.
...Rf7 or ...Rf8 leads to forced captures and attacks against the white king. ...exd4 leads to a different immediate liquidation. The analysed value rests on those concrete lines.
g3 changes the forcing options for ...Qc1+ and the captures around White's king. Rxg8+ and Qe6+ yield a concrete material consequence.
The checks matter for safe king placement, but the leading lines give White similar lasting activity with the c-file and queenside passed-pawn potential. The tactical margin is uncertain.
Ne4 prevents the same ...e4 and ...Bxb2 sequence admitted by other moves. The advanced h3 pawn and Black's queenside lever remain strategic concerns even after White finds the defence.
The two bishops and pawn relationships govern the f4 break and the pressure on h6. The most direct captures in the short lines do not establish the tactical margin.
...a4 creates the lasting rook entry on b2 while ...Rb4 and ...Re8 permit different pawn and file play. The ordinary exchanges do not display a decisive forcing mechanism.
...Rxb1 changes the sequence on g6 and permits ...Qf2+ after the exchanges. The near-term calculation around the king dominates.
...Qc7 makes Qxb7 lead to a particular queen trade and knight attack. Other moves preserve the central bishop pressure and allow White to use c5 and the b-file in different ways.
The leading choices change the bishop capture on f1 and the knight trades on d5. Black's supported e4 pawn and kingside file pressure remain useful after those trades.
